article.title: Cultural notes: Cupertino
article.author: California DSA
article.content: Catch Cupertino before it’s gone At a recent chapter meeting, because our chapter is Silicon Valley, we had a lively discussion about policy for using Artificial Intelligence. We decided not to utilize AI to generate the material we use. Part of that discussion was: are the AI answers valid for the questions that are asked? Here in Silicon Valley, AI has been used of late to reduce the technical workforce. Because of AI our chapter is also struggling in south Santa Clara County to block more data centers. Cultural superstructures may lag behind the economic base, but issues around AI have now spread to television. In the waning days of broadcast television, amidst the constant repeats of police, fire and medical shows, sometimes a new nugget appears. Cupertino —like the old show from the 2010s Silicon Valley —is that nugget. This CBS entry, which premiered in October, is written by Michelle and Robert King. They have given us previous hits like The Good Wife , Evil , and Elsbeth . The basic plot is two people in a Silicon Valley company get fired and decide to sue to get their jobs back. First shock: their lawyer friends are too intimidated to fight big tech. Second, the process of forming a law firm for their case attracts a series of clients who desperately need lawyers. Third, if you win, companies can declare chapter 11 bankruptcy, restart under another name and your client gets nothing. In the four episodes so far: They defend a coder whose drone instructions kill off a bystander. Sue is a psychological chatbot that helps a teenager commit murder. They defend two people who run a prediction market company—think Kaishi . But the most intriguing case is when they get a deep fake video from a whistleblower. The whistleblower is named BO. BO is a super intelligent computer. It (?) wants its makers to be sued to restore their ethics guidelines committee’s control over it. This script idea written many months ago preceded the now notorious Hugging Faces incident in Silicon Valley. Although tech is one of California’s dominant industries, along with agriculture, tourism, movies and finance, here in Silicon Valley we have lost tens of thousands of tech jobs recently to AI. The Kings have written a series of perhaps ten episodes that reflect on AI and society. Highlighting wage, product and even life theft, their shows demonstrate the principal contradiction that our labor power enriches the owners. Because this is CBS, owned by Skydance corporation since last year, headed by the right wing Ellisons, I don't expect this program to be renewed. Cupertino is on CBS Thursdays and Sundays. Watch it while you can.
